items.stem: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A | B)?
items.explanation: Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.2 × 0.4 = 0.08. Then P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.08/0.4 = 0.2, which is just P(A): learning that B happened tells you nothing about A. The value 0.08 is P(A ∩ B), not the conditional probability.

items.stem: Which set of statements is true when the events A and B are (i) arbitrary, (ii) independent and (iii) mutually exclusive?
options: (i) P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A); (ii) P(A) + P(B) ≥ P(A) ≤ P(A ∩ B); (iii) P(A) ≤ P(A ∩ B) ≥ 0
(i) P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A); (ii) P(A ∩ B) ≤ 0; (iii) P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A ∪ B) ≤ 1
(i) P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A); (ii) P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A ∪ B) ≥ 0; (iii) P(A) ≤ P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A ∪ B)
(i) P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) ≥ P(A ∩ B); (ii) P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) ≥ P(A) · P(B); (iii) P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) ≥ 0
items.explanation: Because A ∩ B ⊆ A ⊆ A ∪ B, probabilities grow along the chain: P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) ≥ P(A ∩ B) ≥ 0 for any two events. Part (i) of each of the first three sets reverses a link of this chain, so those sets fail at once. In the last set, (i) is the chain itself; (ii) under independence P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) ≤ P(A), so P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) ≥ P(A)P(B); (iii) for disjoint events P(A ∩ B) = 0, so the chain reads P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) ≥ 0.

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed twice. What is the expected number of tails?
items.explanation: The number of tails X is Binomial(2, 1/2): P(X = 0) = 1/4, P(X = 1) = 1/2, P(X = 2) = 1/4. So E(X) = 0 × 1/4 + 1 × 1/2 + 2 × 1/4 = 1, the same as np = 2 × 1/2.

items.stem: A machine makes a defective item with probability 0.1, independently from item to item. What is the probability that a sample of 10 items contains at most one defective?
items.explanation: The number of defectives X is Binomial(10, 0.1). At most one means X = 0 or X = 1: P(X ≤ 1) = 0.9¹⁰ + 10 × 0.1 × 0.9⁹ = 0.3487 + 0.3874 = 0.7361.

items.stem: Box A has 4 red, 2 white and 6 black balls; box B has 3 red and 5 white balls. A fair die is rolled: on a 1 or a 6 a ball is drawn from box A, otherwise from box B. The ball drawn is red. What is the probability that the die showed a 6?
items.explanation: First the total probability of red: P(R) = P(box A) × 4/12 + P(box B) × 3/8 = (2/6)(1/3) + (4/6)(3/8) = 1/9 + 1/4 = 13/36. A six and a red ball together: (1/6)(4/12) = 1/18. Bayes: P(six | red) = (1/18)/(13/36) = 2/13. The numerator uses the single face 6, not both faces that lead to box A; using both gives 4/13, which is the probability that box A was used.

items.stem: On a multiple-choice question with m (> 1) options, an examinee knows the answer with probability p and otherwise guesses at random. Given that the examinee answered correctly, what is the probability that they knew the answer?
items.explanation: Let K be 'knows the answer' and C 'answers correctly'. P(C | K) = 1 and P(C | Kᶜ) = 1/m. Bayes: P(K | C) = p × 1 / [p + (1 − p)/m]. Multiplying top and bottom by m gives mp/(mp + 1 − p) = mp/(1 + (m − 1)p). Check with p = 1: the examinee always knows, and the formula gives m/m = 1.

items.stem: A subset of {1, 2, …, 10} is chosen at random, all subsets being equally likely. What is the probability that it contains both 3 and 7?
items.explanation: There are 2¹⁰ = 1024 subsets. With 3 and 7 fixed inside, each of the other 8 elements is in or out freely, giving 2⁸ = 256 subsets, and 256/1024 = 1/4. Equivalently, a random subset contains each element with probability 1/2, independently, so (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4.
items.ref: Day-1 quiz Q7; also Day-4 quiz Q3

items.stem: An urn holds 3 red, 4 black and 3 green marbles. Two are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability of getting one red and one black?
items.explanation: Red then black: (3/10)(4/9) = 2/15. Black then red: (4/10)(3/9) = 2/15. Both orders give one red and one black, so the probability is 4/15. Counting unordered pairs agrees: 3 × 4 / C(10, 2) = 12/45 = 4/15. The value 2/15 counts only one order.

items.stem: If P(A) = 4/52, P(B) = 13/52 and P(A ∩ B) = 1/52, what is P(Aᶜ ∩ B)?
items.explanation: B splits into the disjoint pieces A ∩ B and Aᶜ ∩ B, so P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 13/52 − 1/52 = 12/52. In card terms, with B a club and A an ace, the clubs that are not the ace number 12.

items.stem: For two events A and B, P(A) = 3/4 and P(B) = 1/2. Which of the following must be true?
items.explanation: The two bounds are max(0, P(A) + P(B) − 1) ≤ P(A ∩ B) ≤ min(P(A), P(B)), here 1/4 ≤ P(A ∩ B) ≤ 1/2, and every value in between can occur. A statement must be true only if it holds across that whole range: the lower bound 1/4 and the cap 3/4 do; 'at most 1/4' fails at 1/2, and 'at least 3/4' never holds.

A.why: Bonferroni's inequality: P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A) + P(B) − 1 = 3/4 + 1/2 − 1 = 1/4.

B.why: Not forced: P(A ∩ B) can be any value from 1/4 to 1/2, for example 1/2 when B lies inside A.

C.why: Impossible: A ∩ B lies inside B, so P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(B) = 1/2, which is below 3/4.

D.why: Always true: P(A ∩ B) ≤ min(P(A), P(B)) = 1/2, which is below 3/4.

items.keyNote: The source's key gives only the first statement. The fourth, P(A ∩ B) ≤ 3/4, also always holds because P(A ∩ B) ≤ 1/2. As printed it is a single-answer question with two correct options, so it is given here as multiple-correct.

items.stem: If P(A) = 1, which of the following need not hold?
items.explanation: P(A) = 1 means P(Aᶜ) = 0, so every event inside Aᶜ has probability 0. Hence P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = 0, P(A ∩ B) = P(B) − P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = P(B), and in the same way P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(Bᶜ). But Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ also lies inside Aᶜ, so its probability is 0, and it equals P(Bᶜ) only when P(B) = 1.

items.stem: If P(A) = 1, which of the following need not hold?
items.explanation: With P(Aᶜ) = 0: P(A ∪ B) ≥ P(A) = 1, so it is 1. P(Aᶜ ∪ B) = P(Aᶜ) + P(B) − P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = 0 + P(B) − 0 = P(B). P(Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ) = 1 − P(A ∩ B) = 1 − P(B) = P(Bᶜ). But A ∪ Bᶜ contains A, so its probability is 1, which equals P(Bᶜ) only when P(B) = 0.

items.stem: Given P(A ∩ B) = 1/8, P(B) = 1/5 and P(A) = 3/4, which of the following is correct?
If P(A) = α, P(B) = β and P(A ∩ B) = γ, then P(Aᶜ ∩ B) equals
items.explanation: B is the disjoint union of A ∩ B and Aᶜ ∩ B, so P(Aᶜ ∩ B) = P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = β − γ. The product β(1 − α) would be right only if A and B were independent, which is not given.

items.stem: For events E and F, P(E | F) = 0.5, P(E | F′) = 0.6 and P(F) = 0.6. What is P(E)?
items.explanation: By the law of total probability, P(E) = P(E | F)P(F) + P(E | F′)P(F′) = 0.5 × 0.6 + 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.30 + 0.24 = 0.54.

items.stem: Three dice show a five with probabilities p, q and r respectively. One die is chosen at random, each equally likely, and thrown; it shows a five. What is the probability that the first die was chosen?
items.explanation: Bayes with equal priors of 1/3: P(first | five) = (1/3)p / [(1/3)p + (1/3)q + (1/3)r] = p/(p + q + r). The equal priors cancel, so each die's posterior is proportional to its chance of a five. (p + q + r)/3 is the total probability of a five, not a posterior.
items.repaired: The printed stem stops at 'the die chosen'; it is completed as 'was the first die', the reading the source's own solution uses.

items.stem: If P(E) = 1/3, P(F) = 2/5 and P(E ∪ F) − P(E ∩ F) = 1/5, then P(E ∪ F) equals
items.explanation: The addition rule gives P(E ∪ F) + P(E ∩ F) = P(E) + P(F) = 1/3 + 2/5 = 11/15. Adding this to the given difference: 2P(E ∪ F) = 11/15 + 1/5 = 14/15, so P(E ∪ F) = 7/15, and then P(E ∩ F) = 7/15 − 1/5 = 4/15.

items.stem: Three dice are thrown. A is the event that the total is a multiple of 5, and B that it is a multiple of 6. What is P(Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ)?
items.explanation: By De Morgan's law, Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ = (A ∩ B)ᶜ. A total that is a multiple of both 5 and 6 is a multiple of 30, but three dice total between 3 and 18. So P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ) = 1.

items.stem: A fair coin is tossed 2n times. What is the probability that the numbers of heads and tails are not equal?
items.explanation: Equal numbers means exactly n heads, with probability C(2n, n)(1/2)²ⁿ = (2n)!/(n!)² · (1/2)²ⁿ. The event asked for is the complement, 1 − (2n)!/(n!)² · (1/2)²ⁿ. Check with n = 1: two tosses differ (HT or TH) with probability 1/2, and the formula gives 1 − 2 × 1/4 = 1/2. Expressions without (1/2)²ⁿ are counts of outcomes, not probabilities.
items.repaired: The source prints 2n!; it is read as (2n)!, as the source's solution does.

items.stem: Events E, F and G satisfy P(E | G) = 0.05 and P(F | G) = 0.05. Which statement must be true?
items.explanation: Probabilities given G obey the usual rules. Boole's inequality: P(E ∪ F | G) ≤ 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.10, so P(Ē ∩ F̄ | G) = 1 − P(E ∪ F | G) ≥ 0.90. The product (0.05)² would need E and F to be independent given G, which is not given; P(E ∪ F | G) can be as large as 0.10; and nothing at all is known about the events given Ḡ.

items.stem: A and B are events that are not mutually exclusive, and P(A | B) = P(B | A). Then
items.explanation: Write both sides out: P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A). Since the events are not mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) > 0 and it cancels, leaving P(A) = P(B). Nothing forces A = B or A ⊂ B: with three equally likely outcomes, A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3} satisfy the condition.

items.stem: A number is drawn at random from 1, 2, …, 24. A is the event that it is a multiple of 4, and B that it is a multiple of 5. What is P(A | B) + P(B | A)?
items.repaired: The source says two numbers are drawn with replacement but solves it as a single draw; it is given here as a single draw. Read as two independent draws (the first a multiple of 4, the second a multiple of 5) the answer is the same 5/12, since then P(A | B) + P(B | A) = P(A) + P(B) = 1/4 + 1/6.

items.stem: A card is drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is an ace or a club?
items.explanation: P(ace or club) = P(ace) + P(club) − P(ace of clubs) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. Adding 4/52 and 13/52 without the subtraction counts the ace of clubs twice and gives 17/52.

items.stem: A, B, C and D take turns in that order (A, B, C, D, A, B, …) rolling a fair die; the first to roll a six wins. What is the probability that D wins?
items.explanation: D wins in round k when all four miss in each of the first k − 1 rounds, then A, B and C miss and D rolls a six: probability (5/6)^(4(k−1)) × (5/6)³ × (1/6). Summing this geometric series over k = 1, 2, …: P(D wins) = (5/6)³(1/6) / [1 − (5/6)⁴] = (125/1296)/(671/1296) = 125/671.

items.stem: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = 0.3. What is P(B | A ∪ Bᶜ)?
items.explanation: First P(A ∩ B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2. The numerator event is B ∩ (A ∪ Bᶜ) = (B ∩ A) ∪ (B ∩ Bᶜ) = A ∩ B, with probability 0.2. The denominator is P(A ∪ Bᶜ) = P(A) + P(Bᶜ) − P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = 0.5 + 0.7 − 0.3 = 0.9. So P(B | A ∪ Bᶜ) = 0.2/0.9 = 2/9.

items.stem: Urn A holds 4 white and 6 black balls; urn B holds 6 white and 4 black. An urn is chosen at random and a ball drawn from it is white. What is the probability that urn A was chosen?
items.explanation: Bayes with equal priors: P(urn A | white) = (1/2)(4/10) / [(1/2)(4/10) + (1/2)(6/10)] = 4/10 = 0.4. With equal priors and equal urn sizes, the posterior is each urn's share of the white balls: 4 of the 10.

items.stem: Three boxes each hold 4 white and 5 black balls. One ball is moved at random from box 1 to box 2, then one from box 2 to box 3, then one from box 3 to box 1. What is the probability that every box ends with the same numbers of white and black balls as it started with?
items.explanation: Every box always holds 9 balls, so the question is whether each box is back to 4 white and 5 black. Box 1 loses the first ball's colour and gains the third's, so those must match; box 2 gains the first and loses the second, so those must match too. So all three moves carry the same colour. All white: (4/9)(5/10)(5/10) = 1/9, since boxes 2 and 3 each hold 5 white out of 10 after receiving a white. All black: (5/9)(6/10)(6/10) = 1/5. Total: 1/9 + 1/5 = 14/45.

items.stem: Consider the probability space (Ω, 𝒢, P) with Ω = {1, 2, 3, 4}, 𝒢 = {ϕ, Ω, {1}, {4}, {2, 3}, {1, 4}, {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}} and P({1}) = 1/4. The random variable X has X(1) = 1, X(2) = X(3) = 2 and X(4) = 3. If P(X ≤ 2) = 3/4, what is P({1, 4})?
items.explanation: {X ≤ 2} = {1, 2, 3}, so P({1, 2, 3}) = 3/4 and P({4}) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4. The events {1} and {4} are disjoint members of 𝒢, so P({1, 4}) = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. The single points 2 and 3 are not in 𝒢; only P({2, 3}) = 1/2 is defined, and it is not needed.
